fixes.explanation: That's it. Joab, David's army commander (1 Chronicles 27:34), asks, "Why should he bring guilt on Israel?" (1 Chronicles 21:3). He's the guy in the meeting who says "Are we SURE about this?" while everybody else is already picking up their pens. He even asks, "…are they not all servants of my lord?"

The text never mentions tired troops. Joab, David's army commander (1 Chronicles 27:34), goes right at the order itself. He says, "Why should he bring guilt on Israel?" (1 Chronicles 21:3). His worry is the guilt, not the road.

Joab never talks about timing. He doesn't ask David for a later date, he questions the whole idea. Joab, David's army commander (1 Chronicles 27:34), says, "Why should he bring guilt on Israel?" (1 Chronicles 21:3). He wants the count stopped, not scheduled.

Right. Joab pushes back, but "…the king’s word prevailed against Joab." (1 Chronicles 21:4). David doesn't call anything off. Joab, David's army commander (1 Chronicles 27:34), travels through Israel and then returns to Jerusalem.

Yes, Levi. The text says Joab "…did not include Levi and Benjamin in the count…" (1 Chronicles 21:6). Two tribes get skipped. The same verse gives the reason: the king's command was detestable to Joab.

Ephraim isn't the one named. The tribes Joab leaves out are Levi and Benjamin (1 Chronicles 21:6). Joab, David's army commander (1 Chronicles 27:34), leaves them out of the count. The text never says Ephraim was left out.

Asher isn't the one. Verse 6 names the tribes Joab leaves out: Levi and Benjamin (1 Chronicles 21:6). Joab, David's army commander (1 Chronicles 27:34), leaves them out, and the text says the king's command was detestable to him.

That's what the text says. Joab, David's army commander (1 Chronicles 27:34), leaves out Levi and Benjamin "…because the king’s command was detestable to him." (1 Chronicles 21:6). He carries out the order, but he's clearly not at peace with it. Joab argued against it from the start (1 Chronicles 21:3).

It's true, friend. The text gives the reason right away: "…the king’s command was detestable to him." (1 Chronicles 21:6). Joab, David's army commander (1 Chronicles 27:34), leaves out Levi and Benjamin for that reason. He had already asked David why he wanted to do this (1 Chronicles 21:3).

Yes. The LORD instructs Gad, David's seer, to go and tell David, and the message is, "I am offering you three options. Choose one of them, and I will carry it out against you." (1 Chronicles 21:10). David has to pick one.

That's his pick. David says, "Please, let me fall into the hand of the LORD, for His mercies are very great; but do not let me fall into the hands of men." (1 Chronicles 21:13). He also says he's deeply distressed, and I think that's an honest thing to say.

Famine was one of the three (1 Chronicles 21:12), but David's answer doesn't mention it. He says, "Please, let me fall into the hand of the LORD, for His mercies are very great…" (1 Chronicles 21:13). That's the answer he gives Gad.
Yes. David and the elders, "…clothed in sackcloth, fell facedown." (1 Chronicles 21:16). The elders are Israel's leaders, and they go down on their faces together. This is a heavy moment.

The text doesn't mention the ark or the priests here. David lifts his eyes and sees the angel, and then David and the elders, "…clothed in sackcloth, fell facedown." (1 Chronicles 21:16). They go down on their faces.

Yes, Ornan. The angel of the LORD orders Gad, David's seer, to tell David to build an altar "…on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite." (1 Chronicles 21:18). A threshing floor is where grain gets separated from the husks. David goes up at the word Gad spoke in the name of the LORD (1 Chronicles 21:19).

They don't run to tell the king. The text says that "…his four sons who were with him hid themselves." (1 Chronicles 21:20). David comes to Ornan, and Ornan bows facedown before David (1 Chronicles 21:21).
Yes. Ornan says, "Take it! May my lord the king do whatever seems good to him." (1 Chronicles 21:23). Then he offers the oxen, the sledges and the wheat, saying, "…I will give it all."

That's exactly how it goes. "Then the LORD spoke to the angel, who put his sword back into its sheath." (1 Chronicles 21:27). It comes after the fire from heaven on David's altar. The angel who had a drawn sword over Jerusalem puts it away.

Yes. David says, "Here shall be the house of the LORD God, as well as the altar of burnt offering for Israel." (1 Chronicles 22:1). He picks out this threshing floor, where he built the altar. It's the same site he paid Ornan for (1 Chronicles 21:25).
